advisor.summary: Depreciation — including §179 expensing and permanent 100 percent bonus — begins when property is placed in service, meaning ready and available for its assigned function, not when it is ordered, paid for, or sitting crated on a dock. That makes year-end equipment decisions a pure timing lever: pull a planned first-quarter purchase into December to deduct it a year earlier, or push it to January when next year's bracket will be materially higher. The traps are mechanical: loading more than 40 percent of the year's personal property into the fourth quarter forces the mid-quarter convention, and §179 cannot exceed business taxable income while bonus has no such limit. Advisory by design — the deductions themselves are modeled through the §179, bonus, and heavy-vehicle records; this one drives the when.
mechanics: The placed-in-service standard of Reg. §1.46-3(d) — readiness and availability for the specifically assigned function — controls the deduction year: installed and operable by December 31 counts; delivered but not commissioned does not.
Acceleration: a purchase planned for early next year, in service by year end, moves the whole §179/bonus deduction forward a year — a full year of time value on the write-off.

Deferral: when next year's marginal rate will be materially higher — an income spike, expiring losses — a January in-service date makes each deduction dollar worth more; the rate differential, not the calendar, is the decision variable.

The mid-quarter trap of §168(d)(3): more than 40 percent of the year's MACRS personal property placed in service in the fourth quarter puts all of it on the mid-quarter convention; permanent bonus mutes this federally, but it still bites non-bonus property and bonus-decoupled states.

§179(b)(3) caps expensing at aggregate business taxable income with a carryforward for the excess, while §168(k) bonus has no income limit — sequencing the two matters for loss-year purchases; 2026 capacity ($2,560,000 of expensing, phase-out from $4,090,000) is rarely the constraint.

authority.note: The readiness-and-availability standard that fixes the placed-in-service date.
The 40 percent fourth-quarter test and the mid-quarter convention it forces.
The taxable-income ceiling on expensing, with carryforward of the excess.
Permanent 100 percent bonus for property acquired after January 19, 2025 — the tool with no income limit.
2026 inflation adjustments, including the $2,560,000 §179 ceiling and the $4,090,000 phase-out threshold.

requirements: A planned purchase with real flexibility on the in-service date.
A defensible projection of this year's and next year's marginal rates.
Delivery, installation, and commissioning achievable by the target date, with documentation retained.
risks: The recurring exam adjustment is the calendar itself: equipment invoiced in December but not operable until January deducts nothing this year, and the position fails for lack of commissioning and first-use records — the placed-in-service test is factual, and the proof must be kept in real time.
A December buying spree can trip the 40 percent mid-quarter test and shrink first-year MACRS on non-bonus property.
Accelerating into a low-bracket year wastes the deduction against 12 percent income when next year's higher-rate income was the better target.
Buying unneeded equipment for a deduction spends a dollar to save a fraction of one — timing only adds value to purchases the business already needs.
stateNotes: Conformity: many states decouple from bonus depreciation or cap §179 below federal levels, so the federal timing answer and the state timing answer can differ — check conformity in every filing state before choosing the §179/bonus mix.
PTET interaction: a large accelerated deduction reduces entity income and with it the base of any pass-through entity tax election — reset PTET estimates when a major purchase moves.
Missouri: conforms to federal depreciation, including bonus and §179, through rolling conformity (RSMo §143.091), so the federal in-service decision carries straight into the Missouri return.
reviewChecklist: Fourth-quarter planning list of purchases for the next six months with expected in-service dates.
Both years' marginal rates projected and the accelerate/defer call documented per item.
Fourth-quarter personal-property concentration tested against the 40 percent threshold.
In-service evidence requirements (delivery, installation, first use) communicated to the client in writing.

client.teaser: When you buy can be worth almost as much as what you buy.
client.headline: Time equipment purchases so the tax savings land where they help most
plainEnglish: Big equipment purchases usually come with big deductions — often the whole cost in year one. What most owners miss: the deduction lands in the year the equipment is up and running. Not the year you order it or pay for it.

That gives you a lever. A machine planned for February can cut this year's tax bill if it is delivered and working by New Year's Eve. Sometimes the smart move is the opposite: if next year's income will be higher, waiting a few weeks makes the same deduction worth more.
This is a planning conversation, not a form. Each fall we look at what you plan to buy, compare the two years, and pick the dates that squeeze the most from purchases you were making anyway.
client.analogy: It is like a coupon worth more on certain days. Same purchase, same coupon — redeeming it on the right day gets more back.
benefits: More value from equipment you were buying anyway
Deductions land in your highest-tax year
Avoids year-end depreciation traps most owners never see

steps: WE review your planned purchases each fall.
WE compare this year's and next year's tax picture and recommend dates.
YOU schedule delivery and installation to hit the chosen dates.

clientCommitments: Loop us in on big purchases, ideally by October
